recipe: Apply repr(C) to any type you expect to pass through an FFI boundary, as C is the lingua-franca of the programming world.
trigger_condition: You are defining a type that needs to be passed across an extern "C" function call boundary.
evidence: Any type you expect to pass through an FFI boundary should have repr(C), as C is the lingua-franca of the programming world.

recipe: Use rust-bindgen and/or cbindgen to manage your FFI boundaries rather than hand-crafting them.
trigger_condition: You are setting up FFI bindings between Rust and C code.
evidence: We strongly recommend using rust-bindgen and/or cbindgen to manage your FFI boundaries for you.

recipe: Remember that zero-sized types remain zero-sized even under repr(C), unlike C++ empty types which consume a byte.
trigger_condition: You are using repr(C) on a type containing a zero-sized type and need to predict its layout.
evidence: ZSTs are still zero-sized, even though this is not a standard behavior in C, and is explicitly contrary to the behavior of an empty type in C++, which says they should still consume a byte of space.

recipe: Avoid using DST pointers (wide pointers) or tuples in types with repr(C) if you need FFI safety, as they are never FFI-safe.
trigger_condition: You are designing a repr(C) type that contains a DST pointer or a tuple field.
evidence: DST pointers (wide pointers) and tuples are not a concept in C, and as such are never FFI-safe.

recipe: Rely on the fact that Option<T> has the same layout and ABI as T when T is an FFI-safe non-nullable pointer type, so you can pass Option<T> across FFI boundaries safely.
trigger_condition: You need to represent an optional pointer across an FFI boundary and want to avoid a separate null-check wrapper.
evidence: If T is an FFI-safe non-nullable pointer type, Option<T> is guaranteed to have the same layout and ABI as T and is therefore also FFI-safe.

recipe: Treat the layout of a repr(transparent) type as part of its public ABI only when the single field is pub or its layout is documented in prose; otherwise do not rely on it from other crates.
trigger_condition: You are exposing a repr(transparent) type to other crates and need to decide how much layout guarantee to provide.
evidence: This repr is only considered part of the public ABI of a type if either the single field is pub, or if its layout is documented in prose. Otherwise, the layout should not be relied upon by other crates.

recipe: Be aware that adding an explicit repr(u*), repr(i*), or repr(C) to an enum with fields suppresses the null-pointer optimization, increasing the size of Option-like enums.
trigger_condition: You are adding a repr attribute to an enum with fields and need to predict its size, especially when it wraps a pointer type.
evidence: Adding an explicit repr(u*), repr(i*), or repr(C) to an enum with fields suppresses the null-pointer optimization

recipe: When combining repr(packed) with FFI, always be explicit by writing repr(C, packed) rather than relying on implicit behavior.
trigger_condition: You need a packed layout that is also FFI-compatible with C code.
evidence: For FFI compatibility you most likely always want to be explicit: repr(C, packed).

recipe: Use repr(align(n)) to force a minimum alignment of n bytes, which is useful for ensuring neighboring array elements do not share a cache line in concurrent code.
trigger_condition: You are designing a data structure for concurrent access where you want to avoid cache-line contention between neighboring elements.
evidence: This enables several tricks, like making sure neighboring elements of an array never share the same cache line with each other (which may speed up certain kinds of concurrent code).

recipe: Do not combine repr(align(n)) with repr(packed) in the same type, as they are incompatible.
trigger_condition: You are trying to apply both repr(align(n)) and repr(packed) to the same type.
evidence: This is a modifier on repr(C) and repr(Rust). It is incompatible with repr(packed).
